utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone. Mr. Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Thank you. And good morning, Your Honours. This is case number IT-09-92-T, the Prosecutor versus Ratko Mladic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. No preliminaries were announced. Therefore, could the witness be escorted in the courtroom. Mr. Stojanovic, your next witness would be Mr. Savcic?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's correct, Your Honour. Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I already draw your attention, Mr. Stojanovic, that 65 ter number on your associated exhibit list, 04635, if I understand well, is 186 pages. I don't know whether you need them all. That's my first question. The second is that the one following that on your list, 05618, that seems to be P3476 which was admitted on the 16th of October, 2013. Could that be that it's already in evidence?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you please pay attention to that. Good morning, Mr. Savcic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before you give evidence, the Rules require that you make a solemn declaration, of which the text is now handed out to you. May I invite you to make that solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please be seated, Mr. Savcic. Mr. Savcic, you'll first be examined by Mr. Stojanovic. You'll find Mr. Stojanovic to your left. Mr. Stojanovic is counsel for Mr. Mladic. Mr. Stojanovic, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Savcic, good morning.

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, before I begin, I would like to give a hard copy of Mr. Savcic's statement to him. It is unmarked completely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please do so. And we'll hear from the Prosecution whether they want to inspect the document first, which they're fully entitled to do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: We actually gave them the document and agreed that this was a good idea, so I think we're in good shape.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It can be given to the witness right away. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Savcic, for the record, would you please tell us your full name.

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC
utterances.text: My name is Milomir Savcic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Savcic, have you given a statement to the Defence team of Mr. Radovan Karadzic in writing in response to questions that were put to you?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we call up in e-court 65 ter 1D04806.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Savcic, you have your statement in hard copy as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we look in the last page. Could we look at the last page of this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Savcic, do you recognise the signature on this page? Whose is it?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC
utterances.text: It's my signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: The date that we see here, is it written in your hand?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Savcic, let us focus now on paragraph 46 of your statement. May I ask you: During proofing, did you tell me that for the sake of precision and accuracy, it would be necessary behind the words "in connection with" to add "intentions to attack"?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Leaving the rest of the paragraph unchanged?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: And I would ask you now to look at paragraph 48. In relation to this paragraph, did you tell me that for the sake of precision and better overview of the documents, it would be necessary to add behind the words "compiled by," "the commander of the 285th iblbr, Avdo Palic, pursuant to the order dated 26 June 1995 issued by Major Ramiz Becirovic," and then the rest of the text.

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Now with these corrections and now that you have given the solemn declaration, if I were to put to you the same questions, would your answers be identical and would they reflect your best knowledge of these events and your best recollection?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I should like to tender the statement of Witness Milomir Savcic, 1D04806.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit D968, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: In the absence of any objections, admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So this would be the right moment, Your Honours, to tender also the accompanying documents with the proviso that some of the documents on our list will not be tendered for understandable reasons. I tender, therefore, 65 ter 04119. And we do not tender 04635, rules of the brigade, because it will be used also with our expert witness. We also do not tender 05618 because it has number 53476 [as interpreted]. And then we tender 65 ter 05685, 1D03735, 1D04807. We do not tender 1D04808 because it's not necessary considering that two items of the rules for snipers are fully quoted in Mr. Savcic's statement. And then we tender the remaining three documents: 1D05318, then 23905, and 26060.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, would you please reserve seven numbers, make a short list for the ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, could you please reserve seven numbers and make a short list which numbers would be assigned to what exhibits.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Numbers reserved will be Exhibits D969 through to Exhibits D975.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I hear of no objections. There are no objections against admission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, just one -- one clarification. You said you will not tender 65 ter 4635 -- no, sorry. 65 ter 5618 because it has number P53476. Is that -- that is what you said and it's on the record, but we are of the view that it is P3476. The first digit.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's correct, Your Honour. That's perfectly right. And I have just been told page 5, line 1 of the transcript, the correct number is P3476. Thank you for your assistance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I would now like to read out the short summary of this witness's statement. Witness Milomir Savcic is a professional military man who was in active-duty service until 2002 when he retired in the rank of lieutenant-general. When the war broke out, he was in Sarajevo working as lecturer in the military school located in Marsal Tito barracks. He testifies about attacks on the barracks and units of the JNA during those days by Muslim forces and about their positions in the urban core of the city of Sarajevo from where they attacked with artillery weapons, snipers, and anti-armour weapons. After leaving Sarajevo, he joined the VRS, and beginning with September 1992 until the end of the war, he served as commander of the 65th Protection Motorised Regiment of the Main Staff of the VRS. His unit took part in battles throughout Bosnia-Herzegovina and discharged regular missions protecting the installations and facilities of the Main Staff of the VRS, in securing the movement of humanitarian convoys in the zones of contact between the warring parties and combat operations, and in the disarmament and arrest of numerous paramilitary units. The unit took part in combat in the outer ring around Sarajevo in which fighting he was himself seriously wounded in 1994 and spent time receiving treatment until June 1995. On 26 June 1995, the 28th Division of the BH Army launched an attack from the protected areas of Srebrenica and Zepa against the headquarters of the Main Staff of the VRS. The target of attack by these units, according to available intelligence, was to take purely Serb territories, to cut off the main road from Sarajevo to Zvornik, to achieve joint co-ordinated action lifting the blockade from Sarajevo, linking up with Muslim forces from Tuzla and Kladanj, and bringing Serb forces in a very disadvantageous tactical position. He testifies about reconnaissance activities facing Zepa and the order to attack on the axis towards Zepa on the -- of the 14th July 1995. He was fully engaged in this fighting until about 25 July 1995. Further, he testifies in detail about the document of 13th July 1995 entitled: Procedure on the treatment of prisoners of war that was allegedly sent by the forward command post of the 65th Protection Regiment under his name. Without going into the authenticity and the authorship of this document, he explains the rules used by the VRS to govern this issue as a fully legitimate procedure followed by any army in such a situation. He compares this document with the documents of the Main Staff of the VRS from that period and maintains that all these documents confirm his conviction that the order of the 13th of July, 1995, has absolutely no relation to any plan to liquidate prisoners. That was the summary of Witness Savcic's statement. With your leave, I will put several questions to Mr. Savcic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Savcic, I would like to call up paragraph 33 in your statement. I would like to see that on the screen. The number is D968. In this paragraph, you talk about your activities and the activities of your unit when it came to the elimination of paramilitary groups. During the war, did you receive such orders, such specific orders, from General Mladic directly? And I'm talking about dealing with paramilitary formations.

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please tell the Trial Chamber something about those situations?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC
utterances.text: It happened on several occasions. I received direct orders from the commander of the Main Staff. In those orders, he would specify the location of those paramilitary units, what kind of obstruction they posed, and what kind of problems they created in the territory where they were located, and he would warn me to follow a certain procedure, that I should first issue a warning, asking for their IDs, and so on and so forth. I -- in other words, I should follow the rules of the military police. He always suggested that I should get in touch with the local commander, with the police, the Ministry of Interior of Republika Srpska, if necessary, with the civilian authorities in order to gather as much information in order to be able to arrive at the right order on the use of my unit and on the way to eliminate those paramilitary groups.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Did such orders lead you to draw a conclusion as to what the position of General Mladic and the Main Staff was vis-à-vis the activities of such paramilitary groups?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC
utterances.text: Yes. From the very outset, the Main Staff led by the commander took measures in order to create a proper army with uniforms and insignia. On several occasions, I received warnings, although he knew that I was not responsibile for the entire territory of Republika Srpska. For example, when I came back from some part of the territory, he would tell me, "Those people there sport insignia which are not appropriate." So from the very first day, they were attempts to create a proper army, with proper insignia, with uniforms, a single command, and everything else that a military organisation entails.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And now let's look at paragraph 42 in your statement. You have it in hard copy. I would like to call it up on the screen. For the record, it is still D968. Mr. Savcic, in that paragraph, you say that you had three opportunities to use 105-kilo aerial bombs as support equipment to the regiment's combat group. To the best of your recollection, when did that happen? Can you give us a time-frame?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC
utterances.text: I'm sure about two of those three occasions. I'm sure that fire was opened on Mosevacko Brdo on the 11th of October, 1994. All day we were engaged with the 16th Division of the 1st Corps. Sometime late in the afternoon or in the evening we took over that facility, the Aspiljska Stijene sector. I can't remember the exact date, but I know that it was in May 1994 when I received an order from the commander of the Main Staff. I arrived from Brcko in that area in order to prevent the Muslim forces in their advance towards the road to Zvornik. That was in mid-May 1994. As for the Gradina feature, that same year, it was winter, there was snow on the ground, so it could have been sometime in February or March 1994.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please clarify for the benefit of the Trial Chamber. Mosevacko Brdo, Gradina, and Aspiljska Stijene, were those settled areas, sectors, features, what were those locations?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC
utterances.text: Those were not settled areas. They were far from the nearest houses. Even if there had been houses there, they were not inhabited because those were the zones of combat activities. That was manoeuvre area transected by either our line of defence or the Muslim defence. Aspiljska Stijene was first controlled by us, then by Muslims, and then we took it over. As for Mosevacko Brdo, it was under the control of the Muslims. We took the control over. And Gradina, as far as I remember, was under the Muslim forces control all the time. We never managed to take over control over that feature during combat. In other words, those three locations were far from any settled areas.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: What made you draw the conclusion about the precision of the equipment you used, as we can see in paragraph 42?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC
utterances.text: I did not make any conclusions. I saw it myself. The tactic of my unit was to get as close as possible to the enemy, to be at a safe distance from our own artillery, if the support of 120-mortar [as interpreted] support was enough and it -- those were our own mortar, then I could lead those projectiles in front of me at a distance of 40 metres. Our tactic was to get as close as possible to the enemy and to make most of the artillery assets - in this case, aerial bombs. And as soon as the aerial bomb was fired, we would take those facilities while the enemy was still in the state of disarray. So this was not a conclusion. This was just what I saw in front of me.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness and the counsel please make pauses, and could the witness please be instructed to slow down.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, you are speaking far too fast for the interpreters to follow. Could you please slow down. Could you please take a short break between question and answer. And for you, Mr. Stojanovic, a short pause between answer and question. And could I just ask you a few follow-up questions in this respect. What exactly had been targeted at Mosevacko Brdo? What was it that was targeted?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The targets at Mosevacko Brdo were the positions of Muslim forces. I'm talking about wooden and earth facilities from which Muslim forces opened fire on our positions. There was a very long line, not just one facility. There was a long line of such features or facilities which were connected with communication trenches, and in this particular case the target of our activity was the central trench on Mosevacko Brdo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, earlier you said that there were no houses there, and if there were houses, they would not have been inhabited. Now which of the two -- I mean, if you say there are no houses, you don't have to explain what would be the situations if there were houses. Which of the two is the case?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You are right. There was no need to add that. There were no houses at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: There were no houses at all.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Stojanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: And now let's look at paragraph 83 in your statement; still D968.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If we are leaving this paragraph, Mr. Stojanovic, I would have one or two follow-up questions. I didn't know whether you had done with paragraph 42. Could you tell us, by what equipment were these aerial bombs? What was the launching system?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I never got well acquainted with that system. I saw it in passing on one or two occasions, but I don't know the details of its functioning. Here I'm talking about fire support from that system. This is not my specialty. I did not know the characteristics of that system just like I didn't know the characteristic of other support -- fire support systems such as howitzers or mortars or any such things.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do you know whether there were any firing tables for these aerial bombs?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I repeat: I have never had an opportunity to get acquainted with that system and its characteristics or features.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But you observed when they were fired, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fire was opened behind the attacking unit. I just explained what the tactic was. I focused my attention on the enemy in front of me and its behaviour. I waited for the moment when an aerial bomb was fired on the facility, to observe the effect of that fire. If the effect was positive, I moved my unit immediately in order to take control over that facility. In other words, my focus, the focus of my attention was on what was going on in front of me, not behind me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And do I understand that the target was a relatively large surface, where trenches were, which, of course, you wanted to hit in the heart, but that it was a relatively large terrain which was targeted?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was an area whose surface was some 100 square metres in all the three cases.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: In paragraph 42, you said you didn't draw any conclusions about the precision of the equipment. Does this mean that -- that what's you told us, where paragraph 42 may suggest that you do, but is it true that you can't give us any details about how precise these -- the use of this weapon was?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't have any other experiences apart from those three examples. For example, Mosevacko Brdo, fighting for that facility went on for an entire day. The 105-millimetre howitzers, 120-millimetre mortars did not yield any results, the enemy was still there, and the corps command suggested that I should be supported by the aerial bomb. I accepted that, the aerial bomb was fired, and after that I took over the Mosevacko Brdo feature from Muslim forces. And later, I learnt that the commander of the 16th Division of the Muslim army got killed in that action; in that location, that is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You told us that the target was approximately 100 square kilometres -- 100 square metres. That is 10 by 10 metres, which is very limited. Now, you said the 120-millimetre did not yield any result. From the evidence which was presented in this courtroom, I learned that a mortar is an area weapon specifically used for purposes of troops in the field to be attacked. What explains now that where a 120-millimetre mortar does not yield any success, that an aerial bomb, which you say was fired at a target of 100 square metres, would have a better success? I'm trying to understand the logic of what you told us.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The logic of that is very simple. Those were well reinforced features. I was -- in a number of situations when a mortar shell hit a facility where I was without any consequences. Do you see what I mean? A mortar shell is not intended to destroy reinforced facilities and features.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I now understand the logic. It's the greater power, explosive power of the aerial bomb which could not be achieved by a mortar. That's -- I understand. Thank you for that explanation. Mr. Stojanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: We left off, Mr. Savcic, at item 83, where you speak about the activities of your unit from 14th July approximately until the 25th July. Could you tell the Court in the framework of your activities towards Zepa, did you have occasion to meet General Mladic?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Could you repeat that answer?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC
utterances.text: In that period, I met General Mladic in that area several times.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: When and where?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC
utterances.text: What I remember very clearly is that we met up Brezova Ravan. It's a feature where the Ukrainian check-point was. The Muslims took over that check-point, and then I took it over from them. That's where General Mladic met up with General Smith, the commander of UNPROFOR. General Mladic was present there and observed and monitored how I led this battle to take over Brezova Ravan, but I don't remember him making any comments or suggestions to me. And I remember at least three occasions where I met him in that sector near Zepa. Maybe I met him more than three times, but I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: And in conclusion, let me ask you this: Did you or your unit at any point receive any orders from General Mladic that you believe were contrary to the laws and rules of warfare?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC
utterances.text: I did not receive a single order that would run counter to the laws of warfare, not even when activities were conducted in the area of security; that is to say, activities governed by the rules of military police.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you for your answers, Mr. Savcic. That would be all for now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Stojanovic. Mr. McCloskey, are you ready to cross-examine the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Savcic, you'll now be cross-examined by Mr. McCloskey. You find Mr. McCloskey to your right. Mr. McCloskey is counsel for the Prosecution. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Morning, General.

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I'll briefly go to Zepa since you left off there saying that there was no -- no criminal orders. Who issued the order to murder Avdo Palic, the commander of the Zepa Brigade?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: If he was, in fact, murdered by the VRS, who would have had to issue that order?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC
utterances.text: As far as I know, Avdo Palic was taken prisoner. It's a long story, and I really couldn't answer that question from what I know. I don't know who the perpetrator of that crime is.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I won't dwell on this, but I think you'll agree with me a private or a sergeant or a lieutenant or a major could not issue an order to murder Avdo Palic. Who -- this would have to have been an order at the highest levels of the VRS or the state, would it not, to murder a prisoner, the commander of the Zepa Brigade?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC
utterances.text: You're asking me to make assumptions. I did have the opportunity to see Avdo Palic after capturing Brezova Ravan. I then went into Zepa but I didn't do anything to harm him. I was not either a private or a very high-ranking commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I'm not suggesting you issued the order, General. You agree with me he was murdered, don't you?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC
utterances.text: Later investigation proved --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness repeat.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you please repeat what you said. "Later investigation proved..." Proved what?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Later investigation proved that he was murdered.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So I'll ask you my question again. For him to be murdered in the custody of the VRS, that order would have to have been issued at the highest levels of military or civilian structures; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC
utterances.text: I absolutely disagree. Any irresponsible individual could have done it. But I don't know either who killed him or on whose orders.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Who did Krstic say killed him?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC
utterances.text: I really don't know what Krstic said.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Let's go to another topic. We've got that you retired in 2002. We know that you were lieutenant-colonel and the commander of the 65th Protection Regiment in 1995. Can you just very briefly give us your career positions from 1995 through the time you retired. But just your positions and rank.

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC
utterances.text: From 1996, I was schooled at the school of the General Staff. In October 1996, I got the lieutenant of colonel and then continued at the military school in Belgrade. In 1997, I was made -- I was appointed to the General Staff of the VRS. In 1998, I was placed at the disposal of the VRS because I was a war invalid and unfit for professional military service. From 2000 to 2003, I was advisor in Republika Srpska for security, and I was later investigator for the Defence team of Dr. Karadzic and later head of investigations. It is part of the war veterans of Republika Srpska that includes the families of war veterans, the survivors, and the war veterans themselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And you were, in fact, the chief investigator for the trial of Radovan Karadzic; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC
utterances.text: You could say that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And as the chief investigator, you had the opportunity to review many of the materials that were provided in disclosure to Radovan Karadzic or materials that he had himself; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And you said that you were a member of the General Staff which we believe was called the General Staff because it was no longer war time; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC
utterances.text: In 1997, I was not part of the Main Staff. I was commander of a staff regiment, but I was part of the General Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska. I can't remember the exact date, but sometime in 1997, to the best of my recollection, the Main Staff was renamed General Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: We see here that you said on page 18, line 2, that: "In 1997, I was made -- I was appointed to the General Staff of the VRS."

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC
utterances.text: Yeah, the General Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And what was your position?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC
utterances.text: I was head of the Security Administration.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And who was the assistant commander for intelligence and security at that time? 1997.

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC
utterances.text: Already at that time there was no commander. There was a chief of the General Staff. And these two services get separated again. We don't have assistant chief of General Staff for security and intelligence. Instead, we have heads of administrations that are separated: One is security; one is intelligence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Who was your immediate supervisor, superior?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC
utterances.text: Chief of the General Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And who was that?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC
utterances.text: At that time, Pero Colic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And who was his superior?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC
utterances.text: The president of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And who was that?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC
utterances.text: Mrs. Biljana Plavsic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So as the chief of the Security Administration, how -- how long did you hold that position for, in 1997?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC
utterances.text: The entire year, 1997. Perhaps until not mid-1998 but the first three or four months. That makes a total of 15 or 16 months.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: As the chief of security, you would have been aware of the activities of the Office of the Prosecutor in exhuming mass graves in the Republika Srpska, would you not?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC
utterances.text: At that time, I was really not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: When you were chief of the security in the -- in the -- in 1997 and 1998, you didn't know that the OTP was digging up hundreds of bodies in the Republika Srpska? You never received a report on that?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Just to avoid any confusion, the last part of the question of Mr. McCloskey was you never received a report on that. You said no. Does the "no" also mean that you -- apart from receiving reports, that you were not in any way informally even aware of exhumation, exhumations performed by the OTP?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Not even informally.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: You know in 1998 the OTP searched the corps command in Banja Luka of General Talic, and General Talic received authorisation to allow the OTP and the international forces to search his corps, didn't he?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC
utterances.text: By that time, I was no longer in the General Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: You can still answer my question, though, can't you?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC
utterances.text: I was not aware of those activities.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I think it's break time, Mr. President, or close to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It, indeed, is break time. Witness, we take a break of 20 minutes. We'd like to see you back after the break. You may now follow the usher.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We will resume at ten minutes to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I can briefly deal with the following matter. It's an invitation to respond to the GRM030, the video conference link motion. On the 20th of March, the Defence has filed a motion for the testimony to be heard via video conference link during week of 20th of April. Considering the limited amount of time before the witness is scheduled to testify, the Chamber invites the Prosecution to respond by Monday, the 30th of March, if possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I take it that it will be possible but we will hear from you if not and why. Mr. McCloskey, please proceed, with your cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Yes, it is. It is possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay, General, let's go back to July 1995 and this -- the Chamber has heard about the code-name Panorama, which I'm sure you'll remember. And just can you remind us, Panorama was a code-name for what?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC
utterances.text: If I'm not mistaken, I believe that was the command of the Drina Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Well, the command of the Drina Corps was not Panorama. It was Zlatar. Does that ring a bell to you? Panorama was the code-name for the Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC
utterances.text: Very rarely was I one of the participants because we used a communications on ultra shortwave, and that's why I said if I'm not mistaken. I got mixed up on Panorama versus Zlatar, but not intentionally.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: No, I will probably let you know if I think you're doing something intentionally. But can you agree with me now that you've had a chance to think about it that Panorama back in July was the code-name for the Main Staff?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC
utterances.text: I believe so.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And so if someone identified themselves as Panorama 01 over the radio, who would that be?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC
utterances.text: If Panorama stands for the Main Staff, 01 should be the commander of the Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. General Mladic? Okay, we can agree on that. Now, let's look at an intercept, and I can't recall if you've seen this before. I -- I -- or whether you saw it as your -- in your role as chief investigator, but it's P1305.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So we shouldn't broadcast it. This is one of these confidential ones.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And the Bosnian printout is on the left. This is an intercepted communication provided to us by the 2nd Corps, and you'll see that it's -- it's -- this is dated 14 July.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Let's go to the next page in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So can you see this, the actual intercept. It's down the report a bit. Okay. And it -- this is -- the -- what's mentioned in this intercept is Panorama 3 and a Lieutenant-Colonel Savcic. It's the Prosecution's position that P in this conversation is Lieutenant-Colonel Savcic. And, sir, there was only one Lieutenant-Colonel Savcic in the VRS in July 1995; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC
utterances.text: Not correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. There's another Lieutenant-Colonel Savcic?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC
utterances.text: Yes. My uncle.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And what was his position?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC
utterances.text: He was the Chief of Staff of the 1st Romanija Brigade throughout the entire war.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And he wouldn't have had the code-name Panorama 3, would he?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC
utterances.text: I don't know what his code-name was, but I did not have the code-name Panorama 3 either.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Well, as you've said, if Mladic was Panorama 1, you'd agree with me that Milovanovic would have been Panorama 2?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC
utterances.text: Probably.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And who was Panorama 3?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC
utterances.text: I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Well, as we look at this intercept, we see that P is identifying himself as Panorama 3. It starts off: "And who wants to know?" P says: "Panorama 3." And then the switchboard says: "Panorama B?" And then P says: "Panorama 3." And the switchboard says: "Ah, you need Lieutenant-Colonel Savcic, right?" P says: "Go fuck yourself, you stupid idiot." Now, you'll agree with me is that the switchboard person basically identifies Lieutenant-Colonel Savcic as Panorama 3 in this intercept, doesn't he?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC
utterances.text: There's no doubt about that, but at that moment I did not have any communications means. I was not connected to the radio network. And throughout the war, my code-name was Krivaja 300. Everybody in the military and the police knew me under that code-name.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Where were you on the 14th?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC
utterances.text: On the 14th, I was supposed to be in the general sector of Zepa.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yeah, not where you were supposed to be. Where were you?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC
utterances.text: Most probably I was there, but I can't really tell you with any degree of certainty where I was 20 years ago. It -- it would be hard for me to -- to say that about yesterday, let alone 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Well, we'll all agree that in your statement you said were in the Borike area on the 13th with General Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC
utterances.text: Yes, until a certain time. I suppose until the 13th or until the early morning hours of the 14th, but I really can't give you a precise answer to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: General, you've now had a chance to look at this. You're calling the headquarters. The switchboard identifies you, stupidly. You get very angry. It happens two or three times. And you finally end this with: "What a fucking idiot you are. When I come down there, I'm going to kill you," because not only did the switchboard blow it but the guy that he put you on to did something as well. This is you in this conversation, is it not?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC
utterances.text: I'm convinced that I did not participate in that conversation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: You'll agree with me that your -- the radio discipline of some of your staff and some of your officers was pretty bad in those days, wasn't it, in terms of security measures?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC
utterances.text: You are absolutely right there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Now, with your statement, let's go to 13 July, and let's look at what is page 15. It's D968. It's -- should be page 15 in the English, 9 in the B/C/S. And looking at paragraph 52 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: They are both in the English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: For English, yes. We need one B/C/S, one English.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Page 9 B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now we have twice B/C/S. There we are. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Now, here you're telling us about your communications on the 13th with Major Malinic, who I think everyone remembers is the commander of the MP battalion for the 65th Protection Regiment. It's in Nova Kasaba at the time. And that you're talking about some phone calls that you -- some communications you had with him. And in 52 you state that later on the same day: "Major Malinic called me a second time. He said that a large number of the members of the 28th Division were surrendering and that he could not offer protect to his men or prisoners?" That should probably be in English "not offer protection to his men or the prisoners." "At the time he had about 15 men." And then in the next paragraph, we can see that you gave him some directions and to get some more men. Now, having that in mind could we go to P1272, something I know you've seen before. This is another intercept. And this is dated from the 13th of July, as we can --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Also confidential. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: We can see that on the front page. Let's go to the next page in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Sorry, the next page after that. Should be page 3 in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And if you can take look at that. And let's turn the page in the B/C/S so you can see --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: If we could turn the page so we can see the entire --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So you can read the entire intercept. Okay. So in light of the conversation you said had you with Malinic in your statement about prisoners, we -- at 1405 hours on the 13th, you'd agree with me that that's the time when there's many hundreds of prisoners at the Nova Kasaba football pitch; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC
utterances.text: According to Major Malinic's report, there was a somewhat larger number of POWs.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Now, and let's look at this intercept which is this time identified between X and Y, so unknown speakers. And X says: "Where is that?" And Y says --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey, in the B/C/S version, it starts only the last few lines, so we should go back one page.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please restart.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So it -- it starts what appears to be in -- after the beginning of this must have been lost, but they here in -- as it starts: "Where is that," X asks. Y says: "Here at the football." X says: "Is it visible?" Y says: "Fuck, it is." X says: "Brother, don't take anyone. I'll send you an urgent telegram now, don't take anyone ... a little. I'll send you the telegram now and explain to you." Y says: "Go ahead."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Now we have to move to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We have to turn to --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: X says: "Secure it well, and you'll get it now in the telegram. Y says: "Fine." X says: "Cheers." Y says: "I will do nothing before that." X says: "Nothing?" General, is this you speaking to Malinic about the prisoners and you're telling him you're about to send him a telegram on what to do with them?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC
utterances.text: It is highly likely that that conversation involved Malinic and myself, although there's no proof of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And after all these years, and you've had a chance to think about this, so you think this is -- this is -- this would be you, then, X would be you, Y would be Malinic?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC
utterances.text: We spoke about that on several occasions. The fact is that we did speak on two occasions on that day. It's very difficult for me to remember the contents of those conversations, but it is highly likely that it is, indeed, a conversation between the two of us.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: X being you; Y being Malinic?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC
utterances.text: Probably.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Well, Malinic wouldn't be issuing you instructions, would he?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC
utterances.text: You're right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And perhaps to add to that, you were not at the football at that time, were you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, you're right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So where Y says, "Here at the football," would that allow for the conclusion that if this is Malinic, that Y is Malinic because he was at the football?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Probably. Or he was very close to the football pitch.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Let's go back to your statement, D968, page 16 now in the English, page 9 in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: It's paragraph 56 I want to look at.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And here, you were saying: "I was shown proof, P168."

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And, for the record, Mr. President, this is Mladic, P1558, and this is the document, I'll soon have it up on the board, that we will hopefully all remember to be the 13 July proposal that comes out in Mr. Savcic's name dated 13 July, related to the prisoners at Nova Kasaba.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And you say: "According to its contents, this document can be considered as a military document - telegram." So we have now seen the conversation between you and Malinic where you tell him you're going to be sending him a telegram about the subject matter of the conversation, the prisoners mainly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Could we have this document on the screen, P1558.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, I wish I had two screens, but it would be helpful to have that one to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What you would like to have on the other one? The statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Ideally the statement, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We all have a -- yes, we leave it in your hands when you want to switch from one to the other, but we have, of course, the statement, and the witness has the statement before him. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. I think and that's -- I probably have this document etched in my head, but let's get it on the screen because I don't always trust what's etched in my head. So, yes, P1558.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And we see that this is the IKM 65th Motorised Protection Regiment Borike, 1400 hours, and I'll remind everyone that the P1272, the conversation between you and Malinic, was noted by the 2nd Corps at 1405 hours, same date. This is entitled: "Procedure for Treatment of War Prisoners." And we can see that it's to the commander of the Main Staff, who we agree is Mladic, for his information. And then to the assistant commander for morale, religious, and legal affairs who I'm sure you'll agree is General Gvero, for his information, and the commander of the military police battalion of the 65th Protection Regiment, who I'm sure you'll agree is Major Malinic. And it talks about in the beginning there are over 1.000 members of the former 28th Division of the so-called BiH army captured in the area of Dusanovo, Kasaba, the prisoners are under the control of the military police battalion of the 65th Protection Regiment. Let's go to the next page in the English. And we can all see that it's from Commander Lieutenant-Colonel Milomir Savcic. Now, Colonel -- excuse me, General, getting back to your statement, you refer to this document in paragraph 56 as a telegram, and you have acknowledged the conversation to -- happened at about the same time that this -- of the date on the top of this telegram, and time at the top of the telegram. And then you go on and say in paragraph 56: "In its form, it is absolutely unacceptable. There is no number and it is not signed. It is very disputable in that respect. It just sounds incredible to me that a communications operation dared to process, encode, and forward such a document. This procedure is strictly regulated and registers must know who sent the telegram, without any doubt." But then if we go to next page, page 16 in English, page 10 in the B/C/S, looking at paragraph 60, it says, referring to the same document: "The document says that it conveys a message from an assistant commander for intelligence and security of the VRS. This was the post of General Tolimir. I do not remember the general forwarding this document to me, but I can't [sic] rule it out as a possibility. If he had, it was of no importance to me and it is highly likely that I would not remember it if I were asked about it for the first time ten years later." Now, Mr. Stojanovic said in the summary that, when speaking of this document, without going into the authentication of the document, you talk about it. But what I want to ask you about is: Here you referred to the document as unacceptable, in paragraph 56, and seem to be challenging it, but then you go on to say that you can't rule it out. So I'm asking you about authenticity now. What is your position? Is this an authentic document?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC
utterances.text: As I've already stated -- you're an experienced attorney, you have been working for a number of years, I don't know what your attitude is towards a document which is not signed, which has not been recorded, so I have my doubts about it. Your question was a bit broader. But for example, in the document in the heading thereof, it says that it was drafted at the IKM of the 65th Motorised Protection Regiment. If you look at the rules and if you see what an IKM implies, you will see that there was no IKM there. So this information is incorrect also.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, you are repeating what is in your statement already. The simple question was whether you are in a position to say that this document is an authentic document or not or that are you not in a position to confirm that or to deny that. All the rest is argument, conclusions, opinion. Do you know or do you not know whether this is an authentic document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I cannot confirm the authenticity, but I also cannot say that it is not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. That's clear. You have no final -- you can't for a fact confirm that this is an original document, neither can you deny, that it is. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And I'll just have a couple of clarifying questions on this. I do have the original document, which is -- the witness knows came from the Drina Corps collection, if anyone would like to see it. We -- I may ask a question or two about it, and I would like the witness to have it before him for the questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, and I would like to see it before it is given to the witness. So does Mr. Stojanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, just one question. I would like to show the original document to General Mladic. Can I -- do I have your leave to do that, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, of course. The accused will have access to the original document as well. Please proceed, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: You just said back on page 31 about what an IKM implies and that -- you said: "... you will see that there was no," I think you meant, "IKM there. So this information is incorrect also." Let me briefly go to 65 ter 32250. This is a transcript of our interview many years ago, back in 2005. Should be page 29 in e-court in the English and page 43 in the B/C/S. And we are talking about this document. And I say to you: "Okay. So, I really -- I need you to help me with this. You think this is a document that was created falsely and placed in the Drina archives [sic]? Or is it something ..." And your answer is: "I doubt it was falsified. I mean, to be honest, I don't know. I am closer to the truth if I say that this is authentic document, but if you allow me, I really, I can't remember ..." Do you stand by this statement, especially the part about to be closer to the truth that it's authentic?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC
utterances.text: No, I was not really saying definitively that it's not authentic and I'm not 100 per cent sure either that it's a forgery. There are nuances to my answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: General, my question wasn't very nuanced. Do you stand by what you told me. It's right in front of you on the screen?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC
utterances.text: I just said that a moment ago. You will agree that the first time I saw that document in 2003. The first answer does not always have to be the best answer, especially if you treat the person as a suspect. He sometimes answer in not exactly the best way.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Fair enough. And that's why I asked you: Do you stand by your answer when you said, "I doubt it was falsified"? That particular part. Do you stand by that? To this day, do you still doubt it was falsified?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC
utterances.text: Well, I said a moment ago I can't confirm either way. I don't understand why you keep asking me the same question 100 times.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, let's -- finally the Chamber will determine whether or not it's an authentic document. I think there's a slight difference with what you said when you were interviewed. If I understood your words well, you said at the time that you considered it more likely that it was authentic, although you do not know for sure, than you considered it likely it to be a forgery. Do you stand by what you said then, that you considered it more likely to be authentic than to be a forgery?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I stand behind what I said earlier today. I think it's closer to the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, earlier today you said you don't know. And when -- because you say "I can neither confirm nor deny." Well, that's the same in your previous statement. In the previous statement, however, you express yourself on the likelihood of it being authentic or -- it being a forgery. Do you still stand by the -- what you said at the time as it being more likely to be authentic than to be a forgery?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I really don't know what to answer. If I say that I stand behind what I said earlier today, and that it's closer to the truth, these are very small nuances. Even back then I didn't guarantee it was either falsified or authentic. I don't remember drafting that document and I don't believe that anyone forged it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You are skillfully evading to answer the question. The question is whether you still, as you expressed at the time, apart from not being able to say whether it's authentic or not, whether you still today stand behind your statement given then, that you consider it more likely than not to be authentic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I answered a moment ago that it was my first answer to that question, and it might not have been the best.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Okay. Please let's move on, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I do want to keep reading down here a bit because we -- you started talking about the IKM issue that you just -- I just mentioned to you. I say on line 7: "Let's go over it a little bit," meaning the document? You tell me to go ahead. And I say: "It says IKM Borike at 1400 hours. And you already told us that this was the period of time, there is an IKM at Borike and that's where you are." And then you say: "IKM is where the commander is, so if I were there that's called forward command post." And then I say: "Right. So we know such a thing exists?" And you say: "That's for sure. I'm there." So that's quite a bit different from your comment about the forward command post that you just made under oath, which is the -- which is correct?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey, you're creating confusion. Because the witness today also says that he was there but there was no IKM. So you should split up that clearly when you say was it true what you said at the time, because to some extent it is the same and to some extent it is not the same. So you should clearly identify exactly what you're seeking the witness to confirm or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All I'm concerned about -- we all know you were there, it's not an issue. You said that you contested that there was an IKM there, and in this one you're confirming there is. Is there or is there not an IKM at Borike at the time?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC
utterances.text: At Borike, no IKM of the regiment had been developed but I was there, and I'm not disputing that for a moment. If you look at the extract from the rules and the concept of the IKM, you will see that one person cannot make up an IKM regardless of whether he was a commander or a member of the command. And precisely for that reason, that I was alone and had no assistants with me, I dispute that it was an IKM as defined by the rules. Nothing else. So I'm not disputing for a moment that I was there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey, here again in the statement we find not "forward command post" but -- not "forward command post" but a "formal forward command post," the formal IKM. It seems that the witness is saying according to the rules, he now says, and apparently he was there, that's clear, there's now a word play of whether if the IKM was formally there in accordance with the rules or not, or whether the witness, as he said at the time, if the commander is there, there's an IKM, but he didn't add to that that it would be a formal IKM. We are playing with words at this moment and I think that it doesn't assist us greatly. It's relatively clear, I think, that the witness is withdrawing that there was a formal IKM, and that all in the context of apparently an argument about the authenticity of a document which clear says IKM. That's apparently the issue. I'd suggest that we not stay too long with this. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, it's the Prosecution's position that this is a very important document. And I'm making my best effort to identify the very few factors he has used to undercut this document. That's all I'm doing. But perhaps --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, you may proceed. Also the Chamber -- what I expressed just a minute ago, I did it as Presiding Judge of this Chamber, but it might not be fully agreed by all of my colleagues, which means that you can proceed as you consider appropriate.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I actually agree with everything you said, Mr. President. I just -- the emphasis is slightly different is all. So -- and I think we can resolve it if I can just put this one page of the interview in evidence and the -- that issue can be resolved.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Have you uploaded this one page?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: No, we have the whole thing, of course, but we'll get that fixed up so we just get the one page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Could a number be reserved for it?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will MFI P7266, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P7266 is marked for identification. Apparently Mr. Stojanovic is still consulting. Mr. Stojanovic, Mr. McCloskey has just tendered the one page of the interview the witness gave at the time. I hear of no objections. So once it's uploaded it -- that page is admitted. Please proceed. No loud speaking.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No loud speaking, Mr. Mladic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. If we could go to P3467. Should be page 13.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And this is the transcript of the evidence of a cryptographer from the Rogatica Brigade that is in evidence in this case as 92 bis. His name is Danko Gojkovic. And General, you remember perhaps talking to Mr. Nicholls in cross-examination about the evidence of Danko Gojkovic. Do you recall who Danko Gojkovic is and his evidence about the person that actually sent this document via teletype?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC
utterances.text: I remember the conversation with Mr. Nicholls and my answers to his questions regarding the encryptor. The name Danko Gojkovic is a name I heard many years later when this document was first shown to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And, for the record, the P125 mentioned there is -- is the document we're talking about which, sorry, has left my head. P1558. And if we could to the next page after glancing at that first page. I'll -- I'm sorry, I'll get the question -- the end of the question. "The document that you're looking at right now, 125, what kind of -- we see that is a -- we see typeface on this. What kind of machine did this document in your view? "In my opinion a typewriter."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Could that be enlarged. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: "Q. And did you have anything to do with this document? "A. No. "Q. What I mean by that is: Do you recognise any writing you did on this document? "A. Yes, I wrote that I transmitted it at 1510 hours on the 13th of July, 1995. "Q. And is that an original inked signature of yours in the bottom left-hand corner underneath that information you just gave us? "A. Yes. "Q. And did you sometimes use a typewriter in injure job in 1995? "A. No. "Q. Did you have access to a typewriter around the command anywhere [sic]? "A. There was certainly typewriter at the command. But where I worked, no." Going to the next page. And I won't take the time to read all that out. You can take a look at it. It mentions your name. He doesn't have an explanation why there's no signature. And he can't explain -- well, I'll read that question: "There's also no strictly confidential number and it's, as we can see, not in the typical form of -- that we've seen from the other teleprinter documents. Can you explain that?" And he says: "I don't know. I can't explain it. If we only had this same document typed on a teleprinter with a number on it, or perhaps I made a telephone call to find out the number. If we had a teleprinter version of this document, we would see perhaps a number, or perhaps it was sent simply like this, without a number. "Q. But the fact that you have signed and written 'delivered' on this, does that indicate that you actually typed this into the teleprinter and sent it? "A. Yes, yes." Do you have any reason to believe any of this material is not correct, this information provided by this witness?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC
utterances.text: I have no reason to doubt anything. But as far as I remember, this witness stated further on that he had no guarantee whatsoever that I had drafted those documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, would you please refrain from giving information you're not asked for. The simple question was whether you have any fact to your knowledge that this witness was not telling the truth, and then, of course, on the portion read to you, and apparently you have not. You could have left it to that. We are not in a debating club here. We are in a court of law. Please proceed -- well, I'm looking at the clock. Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: It's a good time to break if it's break time. I will get organised and I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's approximately --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: -- shouldn't be much longer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's approximately break time. Witness, we'll take a break of 20 minutes. We'd like to see you back after the break. You may now follow the usher.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll resume at ten minutes past 12.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We wait for the witness to be escorted into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And, Mr. President, if I could introduce a new member of our team, Cody Corliss.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Welcome in this courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey, please proceed. I do understand that you've used two-thirds of your time, until now.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: If we could go back to your statement. It's D968. Paragraph 60. I just want to read out and remind us of something you said about this -- about the document 1558. And in speaking of the -- of the document, you basically say that: "I do not remember the general forwarding this document to me," and you mean by that General Tolimir, as we can see, "but I cannot rule it out as a possibility. If he had, it was of no importance to me and it is highly likely that I would not remember it if I were asked about it for the first time ten years later." So bearing in mind your comment here that this document would not have been any of importance to you even had Tolimir done this -- let's go back to the document, P1558. And we've already noted, and I'm sure you'll agree with me, that in the title there's a specific mention of -- to General Mladic, General Gvero, and Major Malinic. And we see on the second paragraph of the document that the assistant commander for security and intelligence affairs proposes the following. So we have Mladic, Gvero, Malinic, and now Tolimir is making a proposal. If we go not next page in English. And it says once the commander of the military police battalion receives this order, he should contact General Miletic and receive from him additional orders. So we now have General Miletic, who I'm sure you'll agree with me, was the assistant commander for operations and training from the Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So in a short one-page document entitled: "Procedure for the Treatment of War Prisoners" that has to do with a thousand prisoners captured in one day, we have all of these men. Is there anyone at the Main Staff that's more important than Mladic, Gvero, Miletic, and Tolimir? Aside from Milovanovic who was in the Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC
utterances.text: Is that a question?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC
utterances.text: Well, that's the commander, two assistants -- no, one assistant, and the chief of operations.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: My question was: Is there anybody more important than that in the Main Staff than that crew?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC
utterances.text: In the hierarchy, we know the commander is the most important, and the chief of logistics is the number two, if the logistics post exists. In our case, we had no chief of logistics. The Deputy Chief of Staff was not there, so there is no other person in that hierarchy.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So given the subject matter of this document and the people involved in it, do you stand by your statement that even if he had -- even if he did give this to you, it would be of no importance to you?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC
utterances.text: It wouldn't be of any importance. It was not the first or the last time we had prisoners of war and that appropriate measures had to be taken. This content does not indicate anything to me except the taking of measures listed here.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And you agree with me by the end of the day, 16 July, all the prisoners from the Nova Kasaba soccer field, save a couple of survivors, were -- had been summarily executed and were lying dead?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC
utterances.text: I did not know that for many years that followed, but what I can guarantee is that at least in the beginning they were captured or surrendered themselves in a completely spontaneous action, without any prior order. In Kasaba there was a battalion of the police that had about 10 or 15 soldiers in that area at the time --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Excuse me, General, were they all dead, the guys from the Kasaba field? Were they all dead by the evening of the 16th, murdered?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC
utterances.text: I didn't know that for a long, long time. And to confirm that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, no one asked you what you knew at the time. Mr. McCloskey is seeking your answer to his question whether you know now that they were all summarily executed in the following days, apart from a few survivors. Is -- do you challenge that? Do you dispute that? Or do you acknowledge that that happened?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I don't challenge that now. Because, unfortunately, it happened.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And if we could go to paragraph 3, the previous page in the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I just -- I don't want to spend a lot of time with this document but I do want to ask you about one issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: If we could blow up paragraph 3.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And, here we see that it says: "The commander of the military police battalion shall take measures to remove war prisoners from the main Milici-Zvornik road, place them somewhere indoors or in the area protected from sighting from the ground or the air." Okay. Now, I'm particularly interested in the reference to putting them in a place where they were protected from sighting from the air. You, in your statement, give some explanations of these various paragraphs. And let's now go back to your statement -- or I can just read it very slowly. It's paragraph 73: "At the time, there was a constant threat of NATO air strikes, and a large group of men might be mixed up with a tactical group and thus attacked from the air. That is why there was a logical reason for the recommendation to take prisoners to a location where they could not be seen from the air." General, are you really saying that a group of many hundreds of men could be mistaken for a Serbian tactical group or a tactical group of some sort and bombed by NATO from the air?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC
utterances.text: I really want to tell you this and to remind you of some practical examples that happened in 1999 in Kosovo when columns of refugees were bombed, large numbers of people. I believe the pilots did it by mistake without intending to hurt civilians, like when they bombed the train. So this danger was absolutely impossible to rule out, and in practice such things happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So you really think that this -- keeping them out of sight from NATO from the air was to protect these Muslims from a possible attack by NATO? Really?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC
utterances.text: I really believe that. That's one of the reasons. And the first reason is that that number of men was secured, guarded by 10 or 15 soldiers. And anyone who thinks it can be done safely for those who are doing the guarding, especially at night-time, has got it very wrong. They should not have been left there in the first place, because a completely different situation is then being created. A thousand or more people, you imagine the percentage, the ratio. So what you are putting to me is not the main reason. It's one of the reasons why people were removed from that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you, General. And, in fact, after their -- after they spent the afternoon and early evening on that football pitch, they were all put either in vehicles or in buildings where they could not be seen from the air. You've learned that from your investigation.

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC
utterances.text: Not only for them to be seen from the air but also to be moved to some enclosed space where they could be better guarded. But it was not just my unit who did it. When you put a question to me, you always omit something like in the sentence where you talk about the treatment of prisoners of war. Where it says Major Miletic had to talk to the commander. So it's not that Miletic approved something. This is all about protecting prisoners of war and moving them into the facilities that -- where they could be controlled. I would not act differently today. I would have to move those people somewhere. I stated here that one of the main reasons was the fact that in 1992 -- from 1992 to January 1993, there were over 1500 Serb victims in that area. It was a blood bath. So there was an imminent threat of retaliation for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, General, and I agree with you. This wasn't just your unit or one unit that was putting these people where they couldn't be seen from the air. These were several units. And as you said, Malinic would have had to speak to the commander, and the commander that would have overseen and organised all this, there were two of them, weren't there; General Krstic and General Ratko Mladic? These are the guys that organised making sure these people couldn't be seen from NATO?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC
utterances.text: You keep on insisting on the visibility from the air. I'm not denying that that was one of the measures and one of the reasons. However, I would like to emphasise that there were other measures that impacted that decision.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Co-ordinated and commanded by Krstic and Mladic and other unit commanders; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, I was not in the area. I did not have a single encounter either with Krstic or Mladic. Therefore, I can't confirm your allegation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: When was the next time from your investigation and knowledge of the case that we could see Muslim men from Srebrenica from the air?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC
utterances.text: Who do you mean, specifically? There were several groups there. Some groups were visible all the time until they broke through to the territory under the control of the 2nd Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I'm talking about the prisoners. When was the next time you could see any prisoners from the air after they were all put in buses and vehicles on the 13th of July? And buildings.

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC
utterances.text: Believe me, I'm not aware of those details. I would only be speculating if I told what I thought about that; i.e., when was that possible again.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Do you remember seeing the aerial image of Branjevo farm dated 17 July that shows many, many hundreds of corpses on the ground?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC
utterances.text: I don't remember that image. My investigation focused on the sources of knowledge as to what had happened there. I simply did not have the time to deal with anything else or to use other documents. I don't even know whether that image was ever made available to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, I'll find the exhibit number for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: But let's go on to another topic, and I want to go back to your statement again, D968. It's paragraph 82, so it should be on page 23 of the English, but -- great with the paragraph numbering. Thank you. And here you are talking about a document from General Mladic on the 25th of July, which I'm really not interested in, though I think we may recall that it has to do with a security measures along the road and other places. And then you state: "Since none of the prisoners from Zepa were liquidated, this confirms my conviction that the order of 13 July, 1995, has nothing to do with the plan to liquidate prisoners."
